entries.lesson_core_move: Delay a continuous-time signal by shifting each key time point, breakpoint, and support interval T units to the right while preserving the signal's shape and values.

sections.learning_goal: Define delay as a right shift and establish the mapping rule for features and support intervals.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Two-panel signal graph showing $x(t)$ and $y(t)=x(t-T)$, where every feature and interval is moved right by $T$.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep a clean Cartesian grid, same axis scale in both panels, and one clearly visible shift arrow from $t_0$ to $t_0+T$.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the exact delay operator: $y(t)=x(t-T)$, and that this moves each point to the right by $T$ while preserving amplitude and shape.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Single peak at the origin moved to $t = T$.
paragraph_plan: Introduce delay as rightward translation in the time domain.
State the algebraic rule $y(t)=x(t-T)$ and explain meaning term-by-term.
Map a tagged point: $t_0 \mapsto t_0+T$ with unchanged value.
Map support: interval $[a,b] \mapsto [a+T,b+T]$ and preserve piecewise pattern.
Preview why examples then add controlled wrinkles: one point, multiple points, interval boundaries, finite support with breakpoints.

sections.learning_goal: Translate all breakpoints and piecewise regions of a finite-duration signal by $T$ with unchanged segment formulas.

entries.lesson_core_move: Advance a continuous-time signal by shifting each key time point, breakpoint, and support interval T units to the left while preserving the signal's shape and values.

sections.learning_goal: Define advancing as a left translation of the entire signal by $T$ while leaving waveform values unchanged.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A simple continuous-time signal with one labeled landmark and a clear left shift by $T$ on the same axes.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the plot uncluttered and schematic; show the original and advanced copies with the same shape and different time positions.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

paragraph_plan: Name the operation and state the left-shift rule in plain language.
Show the simplest base case with one landmark and one translation.
Generalize the same translation to the whole graph and support interval.
Close by checking that only time locations change; values and spacing do not.

sections.handoff_notes: Introduce the advance as a pure left translation; keep the explanation visual and avoid notation-heavy interpretation.

sections.section_title: Moving a Key Time Point Left by an Advance Amount
sections.learning_goal: Move one labeled time point left by $T$ and identify the new coordinate.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; use a single numeric time point or short time list.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image; keep the example symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text choices, one correct shifted time.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If a feature at $t_0$ is advanced by $T$, which time is the new feature location?
distractor_plan: Use $t_0+T$ instead of subtracting.
Leave the time unchanged.
Subtract in the wrong order, $T-t_0$.
Apply the shift to the signal value instead of the time.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this step numeric and single-point focused; the goal is the coordinate rule, not a full graph shift.

sections.section_title: Recognizing the Advance Amount from an Original and Advanced Signal
sections.learning_goal: Infer $T$ from paired original and advanced signals by comparing corresponding landmark times.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text choices, one correct advance amount $T$.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given the original and advanced signals, which advance amount $T$ produced the shift?
distractor_plan: Use the wrong sign for the shift.
Measure the spacing between the wrong pair of landmarks.
Choose the original time coordinate instead of the time difference.
Pick an off-by-one or off-by-half value.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Use the original and advanced signal plots to determine the advance amount $T$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Match corresponding landmarks, read the leftward time difference, and report the shift amount.

practice_variation_axes: Vary which landmark pair gives the clearest difference.
Vary the number of visible features.
Vary whether the shift is integer or fractional.
Vary whether the signals include a plateau or multiple peaks.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the inverse relationship explicit: the learner should read $T$ from the time offset between corresponding features, not from a formula.

Generalize the same identity to $e^{s(t-T)}$ and $e^{s(t+T)}$ so later examples can reuse the rule for real or complex $s$.
Close by telling the learner that the remaining sections will apply the same shift-and-factor pattern to concrete signals.
